content_blocks.text: It is completely normal not to have a dream job in mind. Thinking about specific job titles can feel overwhelming when nothing immediately stands out.

A much more practical way to start is by looking at small, everyday activities rather than entire careers. When you break your day down into types of tasks, you can often spot useful clues about what feels satisfying and what drains you.

content_blocks.title: Everyday Clues to Notice
content_blocks.text: Here are a few different types of tasks to reflect on:

items.title: Solving structured problems
items.text: Troubleshooting something broken, organising messy information, working with numbers, or following clear step-by-step logic.

items.title: Working with people directly
items.text: Explaining ideas, helping someone solve a personal issue, collaborating in a team, or listening and guiding.

items.title: Creating or communicating
items.text: Writing, designing, making something visual, telling stories, or presenting concepts clearly.

items.title: Hands-on and physical tasks
items.text: Building, moving, using tools, being outdoors, or seeing concrete physical results from your effort.

content_blocks.text: You do not need to choose one of these categories right now. Identifying even one specific moment when a task felt engaging or effortless is enough to start finding patterns.

content_blocks.text: Engineering and marketing solve very different problems, but both are central to how products and services reach the real world. Putting them side by side helps clarify what you would actually do day-to-day and what kind of thinking each role relies on.

content_blocks.title: Engineering vs Marketing
content_blocks.text: A direct comparison of daily responsibilities, required skills, and core focus areas.

cells.value: Core Purpose
Designing, building, testing, and maintaining functional systems, structures, software, or physical products.
Understanding audience needs, communicating value, generating demand, and connecting offerings with customers.
Day-to-Day Work
Technical problem solving, modelling or coding, reviewing specifications, quality testing, and debugging failures.
Audience research, campaign planning, content creation, channel analysis, and testing messaging performance.
Core Skills & Mindset
Structured logic, technical numeracy, systems thinking, precision, and adherence to safety or architectural constraints.
Commercial awareness, customer empathy, persuasive communication, creative positioning, and data interpretation.
Typical Entry Paths
Usually requires formal accredited degree or technical diploma pathways with defined math/science prerequisites.
Flexible entry through business/communication study, targeted digital portfolios, or direct entry-level experience.
Common Trade-offs
High technical rigor and longer training paths, but clear professional pathways and technical demand.
Fast-evolving tools and less structured early career progression, but high creative and commercial flexibility.

content_blocks.text: Enjoying both the build and the user experience is actually a very practical combination. It means you do not have to force a choice between purely technical work and human-centred design right away.
Several roles sit directly at that intersection, though they balance the daily work differently:

items.title: Front-End or UI Engineering
items.text: Writing code for interfaces, layout, and responsiveness while paying close attention to user interactions, transitions, and accessibility.

items.title: Product Design / UX Prototyping
items.text: Observing user behaviour, testing interfaces, and building interactive prototypes, with coding used as an exploratory tool rather than production infrastructure.

items.title: Technical Product Management
items.text: Understanding how software is architected while focusing heavily on user feedback, feature priorities, and solving real user friction.

content_blocks.text: To help narrow down which side energises you more in practice, think about where you find yourself spending time when you work on a project.

content_blocks.text: Engineering and marketing focus on very different parts of building and delivering solutions. In simple terms, engineering is centered on designing, testing, and solving technical problems to create things that work reliably. Marketing is focused on understanding people, communicating value, and connecting those products or services to the audiences that need them.

content_blocks.title: Core Differences
content_blocks.text: Here is how the two fields compare across everyday responsibilities, core skills, and typical study routes:

cells.value: Primary Focus
Technical problem-solving, product functionality, structural design, and systems performance.
Customer research, market positioning, audience engagement, and communication strategy.
Day-to-Day Tasks
Modelling, drafting technical specifications, coding, running tests, diagnosing system faults, and optimising performance.
Campaign planning, writing content, analysing customer metrics, conducting interviews, and coordinating promotions.
Key Capabilities
Applied mathematics, physics or logic, structured analysis, and technical tools.
Audience empathy, commercial awareness, creative communication, and data interpretation.
Common Entry Routes
Usually requires a structured engineering qualification or technical technical degree for professional roles.
Can be entered via marketing or business degrees, communications courses, or hands-on portfolio/entry-level experience.

content_blocks.text: If you are weighing both paths, think about the problems you naturally enjoy tackling. Someone leaning toward engineering usually enjoys dissecting how things function and designing technical fixes, whereas someone drawn to marketing often enjoys exploring why people make choices and finding compelling ways to share ideas.
